items.title: Kant gave multiple formulations of the categorical imperative
items.claim: How does Kant's categorical imperative work?

options.text: One simple rule: do unto others as you would have them do to you

Multiple formulations including universalisability ('act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law') and humanity-as-end ('act so as to treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end, never as a means only')
Whatever maximises happiness is morally required
An empirical rule derived from observation

items.reveal:
Kant's 'Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals' (1785) sets out the categorical imperative. Standard count: three formulations.

Formula of Universal Law: 'Act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.'
Formula of Humanity: 'Act so as to treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end, never as a means only.'
Formula of the Kingdom of Ends: 'Act according to the maxims of a member of a merely possible kingdom of ends.'

The formulations are intended to be equivalent in extension but to emphasise different aspects. Kant's most famous example (lying to the murderer at the door) shows the strict reading: lying is universally impermissible.
items.why: Kantian ethics is sometimes reduced to 'don't lie' or 'universalise your action'. The multiple formulations and the humanity-as-end principle are richer — and more humane — than the slogan suggests.

items.title: The Eightfold Path has three groups: wisdom, conduct, discipline
items.claim: How is the Eightfold Path structured?

options.text: Eight factors in three groups: wisdom (right view, right intention), ethical conduct (right speech, right action, right livelihood), mental discipline (right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration) — practised together, not sequentially

items.reveal:
The Eightfold Path (ariya atthangika magga) is the content of the Fourth Noble Truth. The three groups (panna/sila/samadhi — wisdom, ethics, mental discipline) reinforce each other.

'Right' (samma) means complete or perfect rather than morally correct in a narrow sense. Right View includes understanding the Four Noble Truths; right intention includes renunciation and non-cruelty.

Right Livelihood excludes specific occupations: trading in weapons, living beings (slavery), meat (butcher), intoxicants, poisons. Right Mindfulness is the practice that secular mindfulness movements have isolated from its Buddhist context.
items.why: The Eightfold Path is not a sequential checklist. The three trainings work together — and modern adaptations (secular mindfulness) often extract one element from a framework designed to be integrated.

items.title: Modern Judaism has three or four main branches
items.claim: What are the main Jewish denominations?

options.text: One unified Judaism with no internal divisions

Orthodox (including Modern Orthodox and Haredi); Conservative (called Masorti in UK); Reform; Reconstructionist — distinguished mainly by their stance on the binding nature of Halakhah (Jewish law) and the role of modernity
Only ethnic, not religious, divisions exist

items.reveal:
Reform Judaism emerged in early 19th-century Germany (Israel Jacobson, Abraham Geiger), arguing for adapting tradition to modern reason. Orthodox responses (Samson Raphael Hirsch) defended strict observance of Halakhah while engaging with modern life.

Conservative/Masorti Judaism (Zacharias Frankel, Solomon Schechter at JTS New York from 1902) is a middle path — Halakhah binding but historically developing. Reconstructionist Judaism (Mordecai Kaplan, 1922) sees Judaism as evolving religious civilisation.

In Israel, the Chief Rabbinate is Orthodox and controls marriage and conversion law; in the US, Reform is the largest denomination by membership.
items.why: Religions are internally diverse. Judaism's denominational landscape sets up the central modern question — how do tradition and modernity relate? — in different ways.
